chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 241 to 250, Kapilar's kurinji decade on the veri rite (வெறிப்பத்து): mother calls the diviner, who casts his beads and names Murugu as the cause of the girl's sickness, and the friend and the girl answer with irony, asking whether the diviner can know the hill man, whether Murugu is his name, and saying the cure is union, not offering.

241.reading: The friend tells the girl that if mother, seeing the grief that has come on them, has brought the diviner, then that diviner can hardly know of her bond with the man of the fragrant hill country.
241.nuance: வெறிகமழ் describes the man's land with the very word that names the mother's rite, so the land's fragrance and the diviner's veri share a name while the diviner, by the friend's question, cannot know which of them is at work.

thinai_evidence.note: the diviner of Murugu called to read the girl's sickness belongs to the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: she addresses the girl as செறியெயிற்றோயே

242.reading: The friend tells the girl that mother, not knowing and confused into taking it for the god's seizure, has herself suffered sore grief, so it is cruel to leave her unknowing of the sickness the man of the far hill gave, which has paled her flower-like eyes.
242.nuance: The argument for disclosure is made on the mother's behalf (அன்னையும் அருந்துயர் உழந்தனள்): the friend counts the mother's needless grief, not only the girl's, as the harm of silence.

thinai_evidence.note: the misread sickness and the rite of veri belong to the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: she speaks of the girl's own eyes and urges that the truth be told

243.reading: The friend tells mother that she will take to heart what the ignorant diviner says after worshipping the god of the pepper-vine slope, that it is the god's seizure, as the cause of the sickness that has left her daughter's fresh-flower eyes tearful and forlorn.
243.nuance: அறியா வேலன் puts the diviner's ignorance first and the mother's belief second (மனம் கொள்குவை), so the friend's words to the mother already turn her from the rite toward the cause she has not been told.

thinai_evidence.note: the pepper vine of the slope and the god of the hill fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: அனை is taken as the vocative for mother, and the girl is spoken of as இவள்

244.reading: The girl tells her friend that unless the diviner sings the hill of the noble man of the land of fragrant cool groves full of flowers, his veri rite will do no good.
244.nuance: She does not reject the rite but rewrites its song: the diviner's praise of the god's hill would cure her only if it were the man's hill, so the rite is useless exactly because it is aimed at the wrong lord.

thinai_evidence.note: the flowered groves and the hill fix the land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: she opens with அம்ம வாழி தோழி

245.reading: If the old diviner of the town, of a tradition that does not lie, casts his beads, raises the offering and says it is Murugu, the friend asks, is that a kindness to the one who has afflicted her?
245.nuance: பொய்யா மரபின் praises the diviner's lineage only to let it fail here: naming Murugu lets the real afflicter (அணங்கியோன், the man) go unnamed, so the error is a favour to him.

thinai_evidence.note: the diviner's naming of Murugu fixes the hill rite

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: the girl is spoken of as இவள்; no addressee is named, and the household is the likely hearer

246.reading: The diviner has crowded on his veri rite, but the sickness the man of the hill country gave is the kind that ends as the strong tiger of the pepper-hung rock cave ends its distress, by joining its mate in the open ground.
246.nuance: Lines 2 to 4 are hard to construe: கழங்கு மெய்ப்படூஉ may belong to the diviner's casting or to the tiger scene, and the simile of the farmers' truth is obscure; the reading of the tiger's union as the cure is the plainer sense of மன்றில் பையுள் தீரும்.

thinai_evidence.note: the tiger of the rock cave and the hill farmers fix kurinji

iraicchi.act: the tiger joins its female and its distress ends
iraicchi.sense: her sickness, like the tiger's, ends only in union with the man who gave it, not in the diviner's rite

247.reading: If the diviner mother brought, the one who is to know what will come, raises the offering within the bounds of the fine house and says it is Murugu, the speaker asks, is that the name of the man of the hard-to-reach hills?
247.nuance: The question half grants the diviner's word: if the god's name is the man's name, then the diagnosis is right by accident, and the joke on the rite is also a disclosure.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard hills and the name of Murugu fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: the friend's question about அன்னை is taken as spoken to the girl; the girl could equally be the speaker

248.reading: If the angry diviner, having made the sand-strewn courtyard beautiful, is to find the cause by his beads, then fine indeed, says the friend, will be the beauty that is left to her.
248.nuance: நன்றால் அம்ம is ironic: the beauty is fading, and the friend means that the beads will leave it as ruined as it is.

thinai_evidence.note: the diviner's beads and the prepared courtyard of the rite

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: the girl is spoken of as இவள்; no addressee is named

249.reading: The diviner who casts his beads in the sand-strewn yard and tells mother it is Murugu, may he live long, says the friend, for he does not know the man of the haunted hill with shining falls.
249.nuance: The blessing (வாழிய) is double: mockery of a diviner who misses the cause, and real thanks, since his ignorance keeps the secret of the man of the hill.

thinai_evidence.note: the haunted hill and the naming of Murugu fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: the friend speaks of mother and the diviner to the girl

250.reading: The friend tells the beads that never lie that truly the one who afflicted the girl's young ornamented breasts is not the manly victorious Vel, lord of our flowering valli forest where the young peahen dances in its haunt on the gem-bright hill.
250.nuance: The god is described by his own emblems, the peacock and the valli, and then denied: the friend grants the beads their truth only to say the truth they show is not Murugu.

thinai_evidence.note: the peahen and the valli forest of the hill fix kurinji

links.note: Ainkurunuru 241 doubts that the velan can know the girl's bond with the hill man; Natrinai 34 tells Murugu himself that he came to the veri house knowing the sickness was not his seizure (நின் அணங்கு அன்மை அறிந்தும்).
links.teaches: Ainkurunuru blames the rite's error on the diviner's ignorance, while Natrinai charges the god, who knows the truth, with folly for coming anyway, so the pair shows the friend's protest against veri aimed either at the man who performs it or at the deity who accepts it.

links.note: In both the mother acts out of not knowing (அறியாமையின் / அறிந்தனள் அல்லள்) and calls the rite; Akananuru 98 fears that if the rite fails the secret will become gossip, Ainkurunuru 242 says it is cruel to leave the mother in her grief.
links.teaches: Akananuru 98 counts the cost of the rite to the girl, the secret turning into gossip, and Ainkurunuru 242 its cost to the mother, a grief spent on a wrong cause, so the case for disclosure in the veri situation rests on two separate harms.

links.note: Kuruntokai 263 protests to the girl that the mother's offerings to strange gods are no cure and brand her possessed; Ainkurunuru 243 says to the mother herself that she will believe the ignorant diviner.
links.teaches: The same protest against the rite is spoken between the girls in Kuruntokai and turned on the mother in Ainkurunuru, so the pair shows the friend's objection to veri moving from private complaint to the first step of telling the household.

links.note: In Akananuru 98 the velan sings the god's great name (செல்வன் பெரும்பெயர் ஏத்தி) at the veri ground; in Ainkurunuru 244 the girl says the veri is useless unless the velan sings the hill of her man.
links.teaches: Akananuru 98 shows what the diviner's song praises in the rite, the god's name, and Ainkurunuru 244 asks for the same song turned to the man's hill, so the girl imagines the only working cure as the rite itself with her lover in the god's place.

links.note: Both turn on the same line, முருகென மொழியும் ஆயின்: 245 asks whether naming Murugu is a kindness to the girl's afflicter, 247 whether Murugu is the hill man's name.
links.teaches: The decade gives the one conditional two opposite ironies: in 245 the wrong name shields the man by hiding him, in 247 it names him by accident, so the misdiagnosis is shown as both the secret's cover and its leak.

links.note: Both set the hill tiger with its mate beside the velan's rite: in Natrinai 322 the tiger lurks to ease its hungry female, in Ainkurunuru 246 it ends its distress by joining her.
links.teaches: Holding the two together shows the kurinji tiger used as the counter-image to the veri rite: what relieves a creature of the hill, by hunting for its mate or by joining her, is the partner and never the offering.

links.note: Natrinai 282 says it would be fine indeed (நன்றுமன்) if the old diviner's word could calm the bond; Ainkurunuru 248 says fine indeed (நன்றால் அம்ம) will be her beauty if his beads find the cause.
links.teaches: The same mock approval of the diviner is aimed in Natrinai at his cure and in Ainkurunuru at his diagnosis, so the friend's ironic நன்று is shown as a set turn of the veri situation that can be pointed at either half of the rite.

links.note: 241 asks whether the velan can know the hill man's bond; 249 blesses the velan because he does not know the hill man.
links.teaches: The decade's first poem raises the diviner's ignorance as a doubt and its ninth turns it into a blessing, so across the sequence the friend comes to see his ignorance as the secret's safety and not only as the rite's failure.

links.note: Akananuru 388 would ask the velan whether his god goes hunting with blood-smeared arrows; Ainkurunuru 250 tells the beads that Vel, lord of the valli forest, is not the afflicter.
links.teaches: Akananuru separates god from lover by asking about the lover's hunt, Ainkurunuru by naming the god's own peacock and valli, so together they show the girls answering the rite by setting the two lords side by side in each other's emblems.

source_issues: 241-250: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade (வெறிப்பத்து), so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem.
245: the repeated_line flag on line 3 lists ainkurunuru:245 itself among its repeats; the line (முருகென மொழியும் ஆயின்) repeats only in 247 line 3.
245, 247: கன்னம் தூக்கி is a rare ritual phrase (the raised offering or measure); the reading turns on it.
246: lines 2 to 4 are hard to construe (கழங்கு மெய்ப்படூஉ inside the tiger scene; the simile புனவர் புணர்த்த மெய்ம்மை அன்ன).
248: line 2 (மலைவான் கொண்ட சினைஇய) was repaired from sangamtamil.com and remains obscure.
249: line 3 reads வாழிய விலங்கு மருவிச்; the sense wants வாழிய இலங்கு அருவிச் (shining falls), the வ் being the glide after வாழிய, split at the wrong place as in 140.
